title: Stow police officer accused of misusing Flock system to track former partner

reading.body:
This is an access-control failure inside a law enforcement deployment. A licensed user of a camera network and of state criminal justice databases is accused of querying them to locate a private individual, which is use outside the purpose those systems are built and authorised for. The systems performed as designed: they returned location and record information to someone holding valid credentials. Nothing in the reporting indicates the queries were blocked, flagged, or reviewed at the time they were made.

The failure sits at the point of authorised use rather than at the point of technical function. Flock, CJIS and CORI are built to answer queries from people who are entitled to ask them, and the control that is supposed to hold is the rule that queries must serve a legitimate policing purpose. Catching this kind of misuse requires query auditing that looks at who is being searched and whether the subject connects to any open case, plus a route for the person being searched to be notified. The woman's own discovery, after she had changed her identity, phone number and social media habits, is what surfaced the searches, not a system alert.

What is not established is whether Rogers is guilty of any offence. He is accused, a criminal complaint has been filed, and an internal affairs investigation found he used state systems to obtain information about the woman, but no verdict or admission is reported. The Select Board has not yet voted on his employment status.

reports.title: Stow police officer accused of misusing Flock system to track former partner

summary:
A Stow police officer, Jason Rogers, is accused of misusing police databases to track a woman he previously dated. The woman said she ended the relationship about five years ago, changed her identity, phone number, and social media habits after leaving. She discovered this summer that Rogers had searched for her location using the Flock camera system and other law enforcement databases, including CJIS and CORI, multiple times in 2024 and 2025. She also said he drove by her home.

The Stow Police Department filed a criminal complaint against Rogers on July 17 for potential state law violations. After a four-week internal affairs investigation, the department found he had used state systems to obtain information about the woman. Rogers was placed on paid administrative leave in July, then unpaid leave as of July 31. The woman has a restraining order lasting at least a year. A Select Board hearing is scheduled next week, when town leaders could vote on his employment status.
